## Decision and review evidence

# F01 — Alpine APK contract

Status: Defined for implementation; not yet conformance-tested. Revision 1, 2026-10-18.

## Client and protocol baseline

APK v2 package/index format consumed by apk-tools bundled with Alpine 3.24.2; v3 wire format is a separate future capability.

- alpine: **3.24.2** ([release/source](https://alpinelinux.org/releases/)).

Pin actual downloaded artifact digests in the conformance fixture lock; these are deliberately selected baseline versions, not a promise of all historical or future clients.

## Publish / ingest

Admin ingestion of .apk files with architecture/channel metadata; generate and sign APKINDEX generations with the feed key. Package bytes/signatures are preserved.

## Consume and source support

apk update/add/fetch from local, remote-cached or replica channels; architecture paths remain explicit.

## Resolution policy

snapshot-owner per channel/architecture

## Format-specific integrity and metadata

Import trusted verification keys explicitly. Remote signed indexes are preserved; a composed local repository requires explicit regeneration and its own signing identity. Do not silently extend metadata expiry.

## Explicit non-goals

No APK v3 wire-format generation claim; no operating-system image build or package compilation.

## Required client scenarios

- [ ] Publish two architectures; apk update/add selects the correct package and verifies signatures.
- [ ] Corrupt index/signature is rejected; stale remote bytes never masquerade as newly signed metadata.

All [shared source, cache, auth, lifecycle, search, replication and conformance requirements](https://github.com/azrtydxb/Kuvryn-Ant/issues/2) also apply. Task T1 closes contract definition only; T2–T4 remain implementation and evidence work.

## Official references

- [Protocol reference 1](https://wiki.alpinelinux.org/wiki/Apk_spec)
- [Protocol reference 2](https://wiki.alpinelinux.org/wiki/Apk)
- [Protocol reference 3](https://alpinelinux.org/releases/)


# Shared format contract rules

Status: Engineering contracts selected for implementation on 2026-10-18. No adapter is implemented or certified by this planning work. These rules plus each Fxx record replace open-ended workflow candidates; implementation tasks supply evidence before any support claim.

## Source, routing and publication contract

All 26 formats have local delivery, remote pull-through and replica delivery in scope. Local publication is either a native ecosystem publish operation or the explicit admin-ingestion workflow in its record; unsupported native commands are not advertised. An ingestion request creates a staged publish session through the management API, uploads declared assets, validates their closure, then commits metadata/indexes atomically. Requests are authenticated/scoped and idempotent. The React console and MCP use these same operations.

Writes resolve to one local source before data acceptance and never implicitly forward upstream. Immutable versions default to conflict on different bytes. Deletion/overwrite/retention is policy-controlled and produces audit/outbox events. Local signing keys are separate from upstream trust keys. No generic union of signed repository metadata is permitted.

`package-owner`, `path-owner`, `object-owner` and `snapshot-owner` select an ownership unit. Explicit namespace bindings outrank source order; a selected owner stays fixed across metadata and byte retrieval. Fallback may choose an owner on initial not-found, never silently replace a missing version from another owner. Snapshot sources are coherent generations. More permissive composition must be added as an explicit adapter capability with conformance evidence.

## Cache and authentication contract

Default metadata TTL is 5 minutes, negative-cache TTL 30 seconds; digest-addressed immutable blobs live until retention. An adapter tightens freshness for mutable indexes. Cache keys include source/normalized identity/representation/generation plus authorization domain where needed. Unauthorized results are not global misses. Stale-if-error/offline is opt-in, respects signature validity and is visible through explain/metrics. Coalesced streaming, cancellation and range support use the shared core where protocol semantics allow.

TLS is required for deployed clients. Native registry token/API-key/basic schemes map to shared scoped identities; browser sessions never replace package-client authentication. Anonymous read is opt-in. Signing, integrity, client auth and uploader provenance are separate controls. Archive metadata parsing must be bounded and must not execute uploaded code or follow unsafe paths.

## Lifecycle and replication contract

Each adapter maps component identity/version, asset roles/digests, tags, raw metadata, search fields and retained references into the shared domain. Search is scoped and paginated. A full feed seed includes cached artifacts, indexes, tags and metadata unless an explicit selective policy excludes them. Preflight reports unresolved external references; it cannot claim a complete offline replica until required dependency/source archives are materialized. Replicas preserve exact immutable byte identities and authoritative ownership. Tombstones never remove destination-only assets.

Each adapter implements metadata-aware cleanup and health checks plus publish/resolve/cache/validation metrics. Read explain and publish routing diagnostics must be available in API, UI and MCP. Distinct forms of deletion (unlist/yank/tag removal/blob dereference) remain format-specific.

## Conformance evidence required during implementation

1. Execute the pinned baseline clients and positive/negative cases in the individual record; store exact binary/image digests in the harness lockfile at fixture installation. A reference version is a test target, not evidence already obtained.
2. Exercise local publish/ingest then consume, same-endpoint native read/write where defined, remote cold/warm/cache freshness, source ownership, token denial, signature/hash failures, malformed archives, cancellation/restart and concurrent immutable conflicts.
3. Run shared backend scenarios first on disk and the owner's MinIO. Use the same suite for AWS/other compatible endpoints only when needed; do not construct a provider fleet or a full client×backend×provider Cartesian matrix.
4. Verify seed plus incremental metadata/tag/index changes, restart and source outage; every record requires offline closure or an explicit visibly incomplete result.
5. Retain versioned fixtures/results/limitations and document exact client setup. Platform-specific clients use macOS/Windows runners only for their format cases. No support claim before evidence.

# Record architecture decisions and threat boundaries

Parent story: [P01](https://github.com/azrtydxb/Kuvryn-Ant/issues/3). Planning definition completed 2026-10-18. No implementation/test pass is implied.

## Completed planning acceptance

- [x] Resolve Q05–Q09 in ADRs: built-in adapters, deterministic routing, secret encryption/rotation, API semantics
- [x] Specify artifact entities, uniqueness, transaction/outbox boundaries, failure recovery and trust boundaries
- [x] Record rejected alternatives and remaining blockers without writing product code

## Decision and review evidence

# Architecture decisions — revision 1

Status: Decided for implementation on 2026-10-18 under the owner's instruction to resolve technical planning autonomously. This is a design record, not an implementation or security certification. No additional owner approval gate is required for these engineering choices. Product scope changes still require discussion.

## A01 — Runtime, adapters and deployment

Build one Go service with built-in adapters, a React/TypeScript console and PostgreSQL. Use Go's standard HTTP server, explicit domain interfaces and SQL migrations; do not require a message broker, external cache or dynamic plugin ABI. Go plugins add binary compatibility/deployment constraints without a demonstrated requirement; external adapter processes are deferred.

An adapter owns protocol parsing/routes, coordinate normalization, indexing/composition, client-auth translation and its capability descriptor. It must use shared artifact/policy/auth/audit services rather than directly modifying storage. Descriptor fields include protocol revision, local publish mode, remote/replica support, allowed policies, index ownership, signing, deletion and conformance evidence.

Initially support one serving process per independently administered instance, with bounded background workers in that process. Acquire a database-backed instance lease with fencing; a second process using the same instance identity must not become writable. Helm rolling replacement uses a recreate strategy until multi-process serving is explicitly designed and tested. Replicas are separate instances, not additional writable pods sharing one instance identity.

Primary deployment validation is the owner's Oracle OKE with existing MinIO on TrueNAS SCALE. Disk and generic S3-compatible storage remain product capabilities, including AWS and other compatible providers. Do not provision a provider test fleet. A reusable backend suite runs first against disk and the existing MinIO; additional provider evidence is collected when needed. Compose remains the small-installation/development path.

## A02 — Domain model and transactions

Use PostgreSQL-generated UUID identifiers, UTC timestamps, explicit revision counters and foreign keys. Separate instances, feeds, sources, namespaces, components, versions, assets, blob references, tags, format metadata, principals, grants, audit, outbox, jobs and replication checkpoints.

Enforce unique `(source_id, normalized_coordinate, version, asset_key)` and `(dedup_domain_id, digest_algorithm, digest)` constraints. Source types are local, remote and replica; their administrative permissions do not grant feed read access. Feed slugs are unique per instance. Namespace ownership prevents silent fallback to public packages with the same private name.

Publication sequence: authorize and resolve one local destination; stage bounded streaming content; verify declared size/digest and adapter metadata; durably finalize blobs; commit all version/asset/index references, audit and outbox records together; expose only committed state. An index snapshot carries its generation and referenced assets. This avoids a distributed transaction between database and object store. Failed metadata commits can leave unreferenced bytes, never valid partial packages.

Use transaction-scoped locks for coordinate mutation and conditional revision checks for mutable configuration/tags. Identical immutable content can be retried; conflicting immutable content returns a protocol-specific conflict. Mutable overwrite and deletion are explicit policies with audit/provenance. PostgreSQL is mandatory for development and production; migrations serialize under an advisory lock, check schema compatibility at startup and document forward/rollback constraints.

## A03 — Blob interface and safety

Blob operations are stage/write/finalize/abort/open-range/stat/delete with context cancellation, digest/size results and typed capability errors. SHA-256 is the internal content identity; preserve additional ecosystem checksums as metadata. The backend is never the authority for package paths or object reachability.

Disk uses a private data directory, safe paths, temporary objects on the same filesystem, verified finalize, fsync of required objects/directories and atomic name publication. S3 uses configured endpoints, SigV4, bucket/prefix, region, path-style or virtual-host addressing, explicit trust roots and server-side encryption settings. Do not equate multipart ETags with whole-object digests. Multipart checkpoints retain upload IDs/parts; failed/cancelled uploads are aborted or reaped.

Budget streaming buffers globally. Default application buffer budget is 1 GiB, with at most 64 MiB charged per active large transfer; queue excess operations. No arbitrary default object-size ceiling below the large-model workload; administrators configure quotas and request limits. Header timeouts are bounded; body deadlines use idle/progress policy so legitimate large uploads are not cut off by a short fixed request deadline.

Use a 24-hour default orphan grace period plus live reference/lease checks. GC excludes committed assets, active transfers, replication manifests and migration/backup pins. Deleting an unreferenced blob is idempotent; a failed deletion is retried and observable. Storage migration copies/verifies first, journals new writes, reaches a verified cutover barrier, and switches backend references without changing feed URLs.

## A04 — Routing and composition

Feed endpoints are stable for their ecosystem conventions. Management uses `/api/v1`; general adapters use `/feeds/{slug}/...`. OCI uses `/v2/{feed}/{repository}/...`; Terraform uses a feed-bound host with service discovery; a feed may also use its own hostname when a client requires root-relative paths. The console generates valid client examples instead of claiming every ecosystem accepts arbitrary URL prefixes.

Read policy defaults to `package-owner`: explicit namespace binding first, otherwise the first source that owns the normalized package. All versions, mutable pointers and metadata for that package remain with that source; missing versions do not silently switch owners. Raw paths are independent ownership units. Signed repository formats use `snapshot-owner` for the whole configured channel/distribution/component/architecture or repository snapshot. No generic index concatenation or signature rewriting.

An optional ordered fallback searches sources only before ownership is established. Not-found fallback, upstream-error failover and offline/stale serving are separate settings, disabled unless selected. Bind every resolution to a generation/source token so subsequent artifact fetches cannot mix metadata and bytes. Publish promotion from remote to local ownership is an explicit operation requiring a new coherent index generation and cache invalidation.

Write rules use ordered integer priority and bounded selectors: exact namespace, package scope, or normalized path prefix; optional principal/service-account equality. Highest matching priority wins. Configuration validation rejects overlapping selectors at equal priority with different targets; arbitrary regex is excluded. Deny rules override allow rules. The winner must be one local source, otherwise reject before accepting upload. No match uses the single configured default local destination or rejects. Authorization is evaluated separately against the resolved target.

Explain output includes effective rules, winner, skip/failure reasons, source generation and stale state, with permission-aware redaction. Nested feeds are excluded; source references and any policy/template references must be cycle-free.

## A05 — API, retry and compatibility

Use `/api/v1`, JSON management payloads, stable error codes with request IDs, opaque cursor pagination (default 50, maximum 200), bounded filters and ETag/If-Match configuration updates. Keep package protocol errors and routes adapter-specific. OpenAPI and generated clients are release artifacts; schema conformance is a CI check.

Control-plane mutation idempotency keys bind principal, method/operation, canonical resource and request fingerprint. Retain outcomes for 24 hours by default. Concurrent duplicate requests wait for or receive the original result; a mismatched fingerprint returns conflict. Do not replay a response containing a newly issued token secret indefinitely; issuance uses a short-lived encrypted result with one-time retrieval policy, while retaining non-secret mutation identity.

Version 1 changes are additive unless explicitly negotiated. Breaking changes require a new major management API and migration guide. Support the current and preceding product minor for documented upgrades after a second minor exists; never promise a rollback across an irreversible migration. Protocol compatibility is defined by the client matrix, not by the management API version.

## A06 — Authentication and authorization

Implement OIDC authorization code + PKCE (S256) through a backend-for-frontend session. The React app does not persist bearer tokens in browser storage. Validate issuer/audience/signature/time/state/nonce and exact redirect URIs; bound discovery/JWKS fetches and test key rotation. Cookies are Secure/HttpOnly with appropriate SameSite and CSRF protection. Default session maximum 8 hours, inactivity timeout 30 minutes; administrative policy can tighten these.

SAML 2.0 is required at GA: SP-initiated browser SSO, trusted signed assertions, response correlation, audience/recipient/time checks, replay cache, secure XML parsing, NameID/attribute mapping, metadata exchange and certificate rollover. Support signed logout where the provider supports it. IdP-initiated unsolicited login and dynamic untrusted metadata are excluded initially. Keep consumed signed XML nodes tied to validated assertions to prevent signature wrapping. Use reviewed libraries rather than hand-rolled cryptography.

LDAP/AD is also required: LDAPS or mandatory StartTLS; escaped search filters; bounded search results/time; explicit nested-group depth (default 10), cycle detection and fail-closed group lookup. OIDC baseline fixtures are Zitadel and Keycloak; Keycloak also provides the SAML fixture. OpenLDAP provides directory fixtures, with an AD compatibility scenario; fixtures run as needed, not permanent new infrastructure.

Principals and memberships resolve to internal roles. Explicit deny wins; otherwise union permitted grants within resource scopes; absent grant denies. IdP mapping never implicitly creates an administrator. Separate read/publish/delete/configure/replicate/admin. Anonymous read is off by default. Service tokens have random secrets, hashed verifiers, expiry/revocation and narrow scopes; protocol token/basic/API-key exchanges use this same authorization pipeline. Emergency administrator login is restricted, rate-limited and audited, with Argon2id password hashing and documented operator recovery. SCIM is deferred, while preserving external immutable identity/group IDs.

References: [OIDC Core](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html), [Zitadel code/PKCE integration](https://zitadel.com/docs/guides/integrate/login/oidc/login-users), [Keycloak administration](https://www.keycloak.org/docs/latest/server_admin/index.html), [SAML Core](https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/v2.0/saml-core-2.0-os.pdf). Protocol requirements come from these sources; session limits and scope above are Kuvryn Ant design decisions.

## A07 — Secrets and audit

Use AES-256-GCM envelope encryption with a random nonce per encryption and authenticated context (record identity, purpose, key version). Supply the root key through a mounted secret file outside PostgreSQL/blob storage; never commit it or pass it as a CLI argument. Keep active and previous key versions for resumable rotation, then retire old keys after verification. Missing keys fail dependent configuration closed and show a redacted diagnostic. External KMS integrations can be added through a wrapping-key interface; none is required for Phase 1. OKE Kubernetes secret encryption is defense in depth, not a replacement for application-level ciphertext.

Audit successful mutations in the same transaction as metadata/outbox changes. Record failed authentication/authorization as independent security events without plaintext credentials. Audit exports require explicit grants; retention is administrator-configurable with a documented default and legal/commercial choices left to the operator. Webhooks use signed events, bounded retries and at-least-once delivery IDs. Scanners/signing/provenance integrations are optional consumers and cannot block artifact serving.

## A08 — Jobs, cache and failure recovery

Use PostgreSQL jobs with a 30-second lease, 10-second renewal, fencing generation and default four workers. Reclaim expired leases only after verifying ownership epoch; jobs are idempotent and durable. Resume eligible jobs within 60 seconds after dependencies recover. No external broker requirement.

Coalesce cache misses per key in the single serving process; do not claim multi-node coalescing. Keys include source, normalized identity, immutable version/digest or metadata generation, representation and credential/authorization domain where responses vary. Never cache an unauthorized response as a global miss. Defaults: metadata freshness 5 minutes, negative-cache TTL 30 seconds, immutable blobs indefinite until retention; adapters can tighten these. Stale serving is opt-in and never extends signed metadata beyond its valid signature/expiry policy.

Retry safe upstream reads at most three attempts with capped exponential backoff/jitter; no retry of a non-idempotent write. Circuit-break repeated failures and expose state. TLS verification is mandatory; upstream network policy rechecks DNS/redirect destinations and prevents credential forwarding to untrusted origins. Signed external asset links are resolved internally under source policy or explicitly denied; an incomplete referenced asset closure cannot be reported as a complete offline replica.

## A09 — Replication and backup consistency

A full-feed snapshot records a manifest generation and a high-water change cursor. Retain the corresponding blobs/metadata until seed acknowledgement. Transfer verified objects, apply the snapshot, then replay changes after the cursor. Continuous and scheduled jobs use durable checkpoints; duplicate events and tombstones are idempotent. Metadata/tags/indexes/checksums and cached pull-through content are included by default. Selective sync records what was intentionally omitted.

An authoritative source owns its replica records. Tombstones delete only that authority's replicated objects, never destination-only objects; show dry-run impact and require configured propagation policy. Destination policy, credentials and IdP settings remain local. Reviewed non-secret templates are separate imports. Source unavailability cannot prevent reads from a fully materialized seeded snapshot. No implicit concurrent-writer merge.

Backup uses a consistent metadata snapshot plus a pinned blob-reference manifest; briefly fence new publication when taking the snapshot boundary, then release writes while pinned bytes copy. Restore validates every required digest before reopening writes. Data-loss and restore-time goals are in the workload plan. Database-only or TrueNAS-only snapshots are not claimed to be complete application backups.

## A10 — Review outcome and alternatives

Resolved Q05–Q10: built-in adapters; deterministic ordered publish rules; package/snapshot ownership; external root-key envelope encryption; `/api/v1` with defined retry/evolution semantics; measurable workload gates. Rejected for Phase 1: plugin ABI, arbitrary regex routing, generic index unions, broker requirement, distributed write transactions and writable active-active pods. These add unresolved failure modes without being required by the spec.

No blocking architecture decision remains. Exact deployed OKE/TrueNAS/MinIO versions and addresses are deployment inventory, not a reason to stop core development. Product license remains deliberately unselected. Infrastructure provisioning and performance/conformance evidence remain implementation tasks; this record does not claim they have run.

| W2 build fan-out | 64 clients; 1,000,000 assets; 1 TiB working set; cold and warm runs, 90% popular/10% unique objects | App 8 vCPU/16 GiB; PostgreSQL 4 vCPU/8 GiB; 10 Gbit/s local reference network; disk and existing MinIO tested separately. |
| W3 large objects | 1, 10 and 100 GiB deterministic fixtures; 1, 4 and 16 concurrent transfers; mid-transfer cancellation and range resume | Same W2 resources; charge bounded buffers; observe resident memory, checksum and disk/network throughput. Sparse fixtures must be materialized for realistic throughput tests. |
| W4 metadata/publish | 100 metadata requests/sec plus 10 publishes/sec for 10 minutes; duplicate coordinate writers and mutable tags/indexes | W1 resources; compare read visibility, contention, audit/outbox consistency and index generations. |
| W5 multi-site | Two logical instances; 10,000 assets/100 GiB seed; incremental batches of 100 updates; 50 ms RTT and 100 Mbit/s transfer cap | May reuse the same cluster with isolated databases/buckets. Interrupt seed/incremental and disconnect source. No extra cloud tenancy required. |
| W6 outages | DB unavailable, storage full, S3 timeout/throttling, upstream failure, pod termination, lost job lease | Fault injection against fixtures/authorized test data, not production faults. Verify recovery and absence of corruption. |

## Pass/fail targets

- W1 metadata at 100 requests/sec: p95 ≤100 ms and p99 ≤300 ms for warm indexed metadata, excluding client network latency. Record authorization and DB query costs.
- Warm large-object throughput: ≥80% of direct backend throughput measured on the same path and payload, rather than promising a fixed cross-site bandwidth. W2 metadata error rate <0.1% for valid, non-fault-injected requests.
- W2 identical-key cold fan-out: one upstream fetch per key while the serving instance is healthy; restart may refetch uncommitted partial data, never publish it. Warm runs perform no upstream blob fetch for immutable already-cached objects.
- W3 streaming: increasing one object from 1 to 100 GiB must add ≤64 MiB peak application RSS at fixed concurrency after warmup. Charged transfer buffers ≤1 GiB globally; report base RSS separately. Digest/size correctness is mandatory at every concurrency level.
- W4 immutable conflict: exactly one accepted content value; conflicting writes cannot silently overwrite. Every successful mutation has a matching committed audit/outbox event and no partial package is readable.
- W5 correctness: resume retransfers no already-verified immutable blobs; checkpoint processing resumes ≤60 seconds after dependencies recover. Incremental metadata lag p95 ≤30 seconds for 100 metadata-only updates with no backlog; blob transfer time is measured separately against the capped-link budget. Source outage must not break seeded local reads.
- W6 retry bound: at most three attempts per safe operation; circuits limit repeated outages; cancelled or denied operations cannot poison caches. No acknowledged publication may reference unverifiable bytes.
- Recovery exercise: restore a 100 GiB/100,000-asset backup into an isolated instance in ≤60 minutes when sustained restore-path throughput is at least 100 MiB/s. RPO is the chosen consistent backup boundary; backup scheduling default is 24 hours, explicitly not zero data loss. Record achievable RPO/RTO rather than claim synchronous disaster recovery.
- Security/integrity/authorization tests have zero tolerated failures. Performance targets can be revised only with a documented measured baseline and rationale before release qualification; silently relaxing a failed target is prohibited.

## Execution and evidence

For each run record exact server commit, client binaries/image digests, backend and DB versions, hardware/limits, network, data generator seed, warmup (2 minutes), measurement (10 minutes; large transfers until complete) and three repetitions. Preserve distributions and peak memory, not only averages. Report median throughput across repetitions and worst correctness outcome.

Measure warm/cold separately; distinguish bytes actually avoided from estimated download time saved. No time-saving estimate becomes a product promise. Backend/vendor failures must not be masked as protocol success. Protocol suites use the exact selected client baselines in the contracts; add a compatibility smoke for the preceding supported minor when it exercises a distinct behavior, without requiring every client/version/provider Cartesian product.

Planning is complete when targets and methods are defined. Passing these tests remains Q01 and domain-task work; no benchmark result has been fabricated to close planning.

# Select supported infrastructure and provider test matrix

Parent story: [P02](https://github.com/azrtydxb/Kuvryn-Ant/issues/6). Planning definition completed 2026-10-18. No implementation/test pass is implied.

## Completed planning acceptance

- [x] Define PostgreSQL version/upgrade policy, OS/CPU targets, disk filesystem expectations and Compose/Helm baseline
- [x] Select real S3 backend/version targets and TLS/path-style/multipart/consistency cases
- [x] Choose Zitadel plus a second OIDC provider and SAML/LDAP/AD fixtures; no vendor choice is implied by this issue

## Decision and review evidence

# Compatibility and validation baseline — revision 1

Status: Selected for implementation, 2026-10-18. The owner specified Oracle OKE and MinIO on TrueNAS SCALE and clarified that AWS and other providers remain product compatibility targets. Do not create test environments for every vendor. No infrastructure has been provisioned and no compatibility pass is claimed by this planning record.

## Three distinct meanings

- **Product contract:** Linux deployment, PostgreSQL, local disk and S3-compatible object storage, Compose/Helm, standard identity protocols and all 26 ecosystem contracts.
- **Primary validation:** reuse the owner's OKE and MinIO-on-TrueNAS environment when deployment testing is due, plus lightweight local/CI fixtures. This drives first integration evidence.
- **Additional compatibility:** AWS S3, OCI Object Storage's S3-compatible interface and other compatible S3 providers can use the same endpoint/credential/configuration contract. Record provider-specific evidence as exercised; do not call an untested provider certified, and do not make a separate environment for each a development prerequisite.

## Platform selections

| Area | Selected baseline | Validation boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Service OS/CPU | Linux amd64 and arm64; non-root OCI image; build toolchain Go 1.27.2 | Native developer macOS is allowed; production server certification is Linux. Cross-build plus target runtime smoke evidence required. |
| Metadata | PostgreSQL 18.6 primary; 17.11 compatibility/upgrade input | Same SQL/transaction suite, migrations and one documented major upgrade path. No embedded DB. Patch refreshes are recorded in the fixture lock. |
| Kubernetes | Oracle OKE; reference production target 1.36.4 | Inventory actual cluster/control-plane/node versions at setup. Oracle currently lists 1.37.0 as preview, so it is not the production planning default. Do not upgrade the user's cluster as part of planning. |
| Helm / Compose | Helm 4.3.1; Docker Compose 5.6.0; Docker engine reference 29.9.1 | Packaging tests in existing/local environments; no new EKS/GKE/AKS test clusters. Document resource limits, probes and one-writer topology. |
| Local disk | ext4/XFS on a local Linux block filesystem | Verify fsync/atomic publication, capacity/inode failure and cancellation. NFS/SMB/object-fuse mounts are not a substitute for the disk contract. |
| Primary S3 | Existing MinIO app on TrueNAS SCALE over HTTPS | Record installed server version and immutable image digest before actual test/deploy. Reference discovery found RELEASE.2025-10-15T17-29-55Z and TrueNAS 25.10.4; these are inventory references, not an instruction to install, downgrade or replace the user's instance. |
| Generic S3 | SigV4, configurable endpoint/region/bucket/prefix, path-style/virtual-host, TLS roots, static/session credentials or supported ambient credential chain | Endpoint features are probed/validated. AWS and other providers remain compatible targets; optional runs reuse the same suite. No claim of AWS-only APIs or provider certification without evidence. |
| Browser | Current stable Chromium, Firefox, Safari at UI test execution; versions locked with run | Keyboard/focus/a11y plus login/cookie/error behavior. Do not hard-code an obsolete browser release in a year-long product plan. |
| Native format clients | Exact selected versions in contracts/F01–F26 and reference-versions.json | Install and record binary/image digest as each conformance task begins. A baseline version does not imply backward compatibility with every older client. |

[Oracle OKE version support](https://docs.oracle.com/en-us/iaas/Content/ContEng/Concepts/contengaboutk8sversions.htm) supplies the OKE distinction. [PostgreSQL release policy](https://www.postgresql.org/support/versioning/) supplies selected DB versions. Other tool versions were resolved through their official release endpoints listed in reference-versions.json.

## OKE → TrueNAS network and storage acceptance

Record DNS, endpoint port, certificate chain, bucket/prefix, credential reference, region setting and measured RTT/bandwidth. Network topology (private link/VPN/public TLS) is an operator deployment choice, not something the application silently provisions. Use an explicitly allowed destination and network policies; do not expose the MinIO console as the application's object API.

Validate small PUT/GET/HEAD/DELETE, range/conditional reads, streaming and multipart upload/resume/abort, credential expiry/rotation, bucket policy denial and integrity after restart. Verify full-object checksums independently of ETags. Test storage outages and bandwidth limits against test buckets only. Request retries must be safe across the OKE-to-NAS path.

Use the TrueNAS instance as S3 object storage, not as an assumption that the application has direct access to ZFS snapshots or filesystem paths. Application backup/restore pins a consistent PostgreSQL/blob reference set. TrueNAS snapshots may complement it but are not alone a complete application backup. No MinIO/AIStor migration, app upgrade or tenancy change is included in this work.

MinIO's upstream repository is currently archived, and TrueNAS app delivery can differ from upstream releases; therefore inventory the actual deployed binary/image rather than infer it from a mutable catalog label. This does not change the user's selected storage. The adapter depends on tested S3 operations, not MinIO administrative APIs. References: [MinIO release](https://github.com/minio/minio/releases/tag/RELEASE.2025-10-15T17-29-55Z), [upstream repository](https://github.com/minio/minio), [TrueNAS apps](https://apps.truenas.com/), [TrueNAS release artifacts](https://update.truenas.com/).

## Identity acceptance scope

| Capability | Concrete reference fixture | Required cases |
|---|---|---|
| OIDC | Zitadel 4.19.5 and Keycloak 26.8.1 | Code+PKCE, issuer/audience/state/nonce, JWKS rotation, group mapping, logout, expired/revoked sessions and recovery. |
| SAML 2.0 | Keycloak 26.8.1 SAML IdP | SP-initiated login, signed assertions, replay/recipient/time failures, metadata and certificate rollover, attribute mapping and supported logout. |
| LDAP | OpenLDAP LTS 2.6.15 | LDAPS/StartTLS, escaped filters, bind/search authorization, nested-group limits and outage behavior. |
| AD-compatible directory | Samba 4.24.5 for repeatable AD schema/group fixtures; Windows Server AD integration scenario before a specific Windows AD certification claim | Bind/group mapping and TLS; Samba evidence is not relabeled as Microsoft Windows AD evidence. Use an existing AD target if available when the feature is tested. |
| Other providers | Entra ID, Okta, Authentik and generic standards-compatible providers | Configuration/discovery/mapping contract is supported by design; optional provider smoke when requested, using existing accounts. Do not create a permanent IdP fleet. |

Fixtures are reusable, on-demand conformance inputs. Their versions are targets, not claims that environments already exist. Sources: [Zitadel releases](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases), [Keycloak releases](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases), [OpenLDAP releases](https://www.openldap.org/software/download/), [Samba releases](https://www.samba.org/samba/history/).

## Protocol and client test hosts

- Linux fixture runner for the shared core and most package protocols.
- macOS runner only when CocoaPods, Swift/macOS or R/macOS workflows are implemented.
- Windows runner only for Chocolatey/NuGet symbol and R/Windows cases; Windows AD is a separately identified provider scenario.
- A client executable or pinned container is enough where possible. No dedicated permanent environment per ecosystem or cloud.
- Fixture acquisition records actual hashes before execution; security patch updates may replace a pinned reference with a documented compatible patch, never silently alter a retained test result.

## Import/export adoption baseline

Implement the generic manifest import/export first. Define a read-only inventory and dry-run mapper for Sonatype Nexus Repository 3 exports and documented Maven/npm/raw content layouts; the input manifest records the exact source export/version at execution. Credentials are references, never exported plaintext. Unsupported mappings are errors in the report, not silently coerced feeds. Other managers can emit the generic manifest; a manager-specific API compatibility promise is outside scope. Fixtures can be synthetic export samples; do not stand up a fleet of legacy managers.

## Planning completion versus execution prerequisites

The protocol, infrastructure family, version policy, source scope and test methods are selected. Exact installed endpoint addresses, secrets and image digests are gathered only when relevant implementation/deployment tasks need them. Missing deployment inventory does not block core implementation and is not mislabeled as a completed deployment test. Existing scope and source contracts remain the authority; no provider-specific certification is inferred from generic S3 or OIDC compatibility.

# Kuvryn Ant delivery plan

Status: Engineering planning complete, revision 1, 2026-10-18. Implementation readiness follows the recorded coverage/dependency and GitHub publication audit; no additional owner approval gate.
Source of truth for product scope: [product specification](https://github.com/azrtydxb/Kuvryn-Ant/blob/main/kuvryn-ant-product-spec.md), version 0.1.

## Confirmed direction

- Go backend, React console, versioned OpenAPI management API, and MCP access through the same authorization boundary.
- PostgreSQL is required for every installation, including development. No embedded metadata database.
- Local disk and S3-compatible blob storage are both Phase 1 requirements.
- All 26 ecosystem entries in the specification remain Phase 1 scope. Delivery waves do not redefine Phase 1 as a reduced-format MVP.
- Feeds expose stable, format-specific endpoints. Read resolution and publish routing are separate policies. Publishing resolves to exactly one local source before accepting content; writes never implicitly go upstream.
- Phase 1 instances are independently administered. Explicit seed/incremental artifact replication is required; federation belongs to Phase 2.
- License/distribution selection is deferred at the owner's direction. Do not add a license or make an open-source licensing claim.
- Complete planning, questions, milestones, user stories, and GitHub tasks/issues before product implementation begins.

## Planning gate

Development may begin only when all of the following are true:

1. Blocking product questions have recorded answers and delegated engineering decisions have explicit rationale.
2. Every spec section and acceptance criterion maps to a milestone and one or more stories.
3. Every ecosystem has a capability record with named workflows, client/version test policy, source support, composition rules, unsupported behaviors, and evidence required before a support claim.
4. Milestones have explicit entry/exit conditions and dependencies. Calendar commitments require team capacity and workload estimates; none are invented.
5. Each implementation story has a user outcome, testable acceptance criteria, dependencies, task breakdown, and a definition of done.
6. Milestones, stories, and actionable tasks are published to GitHub and cross-linked. The local index contains their URLs.
7. The backlog has been checked for missing requirements, duplicated work, dependency cycles, and prematurely claimed support.
8. Record the engineering readiness audit and verify published deliverables. The owner has authorized completing this work autonomously; no additional confirmation is required.

Planning research and documentation are allowed before this gate. Prototypes that implement product behavior are not.

## Decisions and planning assumptions

| ID | Decision | Proposed direction / consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Q01 | Ecosystem delivery order | Confirmed: OCI/Docker, Go modules, Helm, Rust/Cargo, Raw, then remaining formats. Shared OCI artifact work accompanies the OCI platform. Core storage tests use protocol-neutral fixtures, not early Raw format delivery. |
| Q02 | Enterprise identity release boundary | Confirmed: OIDC, SAML, and LDAP are all required in the first general release. SCIM is later, as allowed by the spec. |
| Q03 | Scale and capacity | Workload-based engineering targets W1–W6; no calendar or staffing promises. See release-workloads.md. |
| Q04 | Deployment | OKE plus existing MinIO on TrueNAS SCALE is primary validation. Compose/Helm, disk, AWS and other S3-compatible providers remain in product scope. Reuse one suite; do not build a vendor environment fleet. |
| Q05 | Adapters | Built-in Go modules; versioned internal capability contract. See architecture A01. |
| Q06 | Write routing | Priority rules with bounded namespace/package/path/principal selectors; reject ambiguous equal-priority targets; one local destination. A04. |
| Q07 | Resolution | Explicit package/path/object/snapshot ownership, source priority and separate error/not-found policies. No unsafe signed index unions. A04 and per-format contracts. |
| Q08 | Secrets | Envelope encryption with externally mounted versioned root keys and rotation. No required cloud KMS. A07. |
| Q09 | API | `/api/v1`, bounded cursor pagination, structured errors, conditional mutation and 24-hour idempotency. Current/preceding product minor upgrade policy. A05. |
| Q10 | Release evidence | Numerical workload targets and reproducible measurement procedure selected; passing results remain implementation work. |

Q01–Q04 reflect owner responses and specification requirements. Q05–Q10 are documented engineering decisions under the owner's instruction to proceed with planning. Exact installed versions, credentials and endpoints are deployment inventory, collected when needed; they do not block core development. No product support or measured performance is claimed by planning completion.

## Delivery strategy

Build capabilities in dependency order and verify each through all relevant interfaces. A usable development increment is not broad availability. Do not start all format adapters against an unstable artifact model.

1. Complete planning, architecture decisions, capability ledger, API conventions, threat model, and conformance design.
2. Build the shared metadata, identity/authorization, audit, blob, and feed-policy foundations with operational diagnostics.
3. Prove the shared artifact lifecycle using protocol-neutral contract fixtures on both storage backends; deliver ecosystem adapters in the owner-selected order.
4. Add remote caching, multi-source resolution, and client conformance. Establish realistic concurrency and large-object baselines.
5. Deliver ecosystem adapters in reviewable waves; keep unfinished capabilities explicitly disabled or marked experimental.
6. Add the React console and MCP incrementally against supported APIs; each capability must retain UI/API/MCP permission parity.
7. Deliver independent-instance replication on stable metadata/manifests, then imports, lifecycle operations, and deployment hardening.
8. Run full release evidence, security, disaster-recovery, compatibility, performance, and usability gates.

Some work can overlap after its prerequisites pass. The GitHub dependency graph must distinguish prerequisites from merely related work. No staffing or parallel-agent assumptions are embedded in this plan.

## Milestone boundaries

These boundaries organize the GitHub backlog. Milestone numbers identify workstreams, not a strictly serial schedule; story dependencies determine execution readiness. No due dates are assigned.

### M00 — Planning and readiness

Outcome: an agreed, traceable, executable backlog.

Scope: resolve decisions; document architecture boundaries and data model; establish format ledger; define client matrix and release criteria; create GitHub milestones, stories, task issues, labels, dependencies, and planning index.

Entry: product spec exists. Exit: planning gate satisfied. Blocks all implementation milestones.

### M01 — Shared platform and secure administration

Outcome: a runnable Go service with PostgreSQL metadata and authenticated, auditable management operations.

Scope: project conventions and CI; migrations and transaction boundaries; feed/source/asset/blob/identity models; API schema and generated client pipeline; service accounts and scoped tokens; authorization checks; audit transactions; health/readiness/logging/metrics; local development and shutdown behavior.

Exit: real PostgreSQL integration tests prove migration, rollback constraints, authorization denials, scoped token expiry/revocation, mutation idempotency, and atomic metadata/audit writes. Secrets do not appear in logs or API responses. Fresh installation and restart work.

Dependencies: M00. External identity provider work may begin once identity boundaries are stable, but browser UI authentication is not considered complete with a bootstrap token.

### M02 — Artifact integrity, storage, and local publishing

Outcome: correct local artifact lifecycle through explicit feed routing.

Scope: streaming disk/S3 blob interfaces; digest and size checks; multipart and cancellation; deduplication domain; transactional publication; protocol-neutral core fixtures; immutable/overwrite/delete policies; source precedence; explain resolution; reference-safe garbage-collection design; browsing/search/checksum lookup; provenance.

Exit: shared storage/lifecycle contract fixtures pass on both disk and selected S3 backend(s); real-client evidence is required in M04/M05; interrupted or corrupt uploads are not visible; concurrent publication cannot silently overwrite immutable releases; metadata references survive restart and cleanup; same-endpoint read/write routing is proven.

Dependencies: M01. S3 implementation is required for milestone completion, not a post-release optional feature.

### M03 — Remote caching and build acceleration

Outcome: runners reuse dependencies through predictable, observable pull-through feeds.

Scope: upstream credentials/TLS/network policy; per-resource cache keys; independent metadata/blob freshness; conditional revalidation; coalesced misses; bounded retry/circuit breaking; negative caching; stale-if-error/offline; safe fallback and source policies; prewarming and schedules; rate limits/quotas; cache diagnostics and savings metrics.

Exit: concurrent cold requests cause one upstream fetch per key under the agreed normal-operation model; outages and cancellation do not poison cache state; stale responses are diagnosable; credentials cannot cross origins; warm/cold and large-object workloads produce recorded evidence.

Dependencies: M02 and format-specific composition contracts. Cache savings calculations must distinguish measured bytes/time from estimates.

### M04 — First ecosystem delivery wave

Outcome: supported client workflows for the owner-selected first format wave.

Scope: per-format protocol, publish and delete semantics, metadata/indexing, source composition, auth, cache behavior, search fields, cleanup, client configuration, fixtures, conformance, and limitations. Confirmed wave order: Docker/OCI, Go modules, Helm, Rust/Cargo, then Raw. OCI artifact behavior shares the OCI platform but keeps its own conformance record. Remaining ecosystems follow this wave.

Exit: every enabled capability in each wave member has versioned real-client evidence on relevant sources/storage combinations; unsupported capabilities are visible. OCI artifact coverage remains distinct from container-image coverage even if the adapter is shared.

Dependencies: M01–M03; specific work can proceed as the shared APIs stabilize. Completion is a development milestone, not Phase 1 completion.

### M05 — Remaining ecosystem breadth

Outcome: all remaining formats have accepted, evidence-backed capability records.

Scope: Alpine APK, Ansible Galaxy, APT/Debian, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Git LFS, Hugging Face, Maven, npm, NuGet/Chocolatey, Eclipse p2, Pub/Flutter, PyPI, R/CRAN, RubyGems, Swift Package Manager, Terraform, Yum/RPM.

Exit: all 26 spec entries satisfy their approved workflow matrices; signing and metadata-sensitive formats pass correctness and tamper/failure cases; no generic file storage is counted as format support.

Dependencies: M01–M03 plus reusable work from M04. Sub-waves should group shared protocol/index/signing concerns and business priority; no arbitrary equal estimates per ecosystem.

### M06 — Enterprise identity and complete operator interfaces

Outcome: operators and automation can securely use the product through React, API, and MCP.

Scope: OIDC with Zitadel and a second provider; PKCE and session security; SAML and LDAP required for GA; group/role mappings; emergency admin; secret rotation; identity diagnostics and recovery; React overview/feed/package/identity/audit/cache/storage/replication screens; MCP discovery/lookups/health/admin tools; webhooks/event delivery.

Exit: provider and package-client authentication coexist; permission-denial and audit parity tests cover UI/API/MCP; destructive MCP actions carry the appropriate client confirmation semantics; accessibility and error/recovery flows pass; no UI-only administrative capabilities lack supported APIs.

Dependencies: M01 onward, with screens/tools delivered alongside their domain capabilities. Final exit also depends on M07–M08 for replication and lifecycle interfaces. SCIM remains explicitly deferred unless scope changes.

### M07 — Independent-instance replication

Outcome: another site can seed a feed, keep it synchronized, and serve locally during source outage.

Scope: peer identity/TLS; manifests/checkpoints; full seed including cached artifacts by default; optional exclusion of transient cache entries; namespace/package/version filters; scheduled/manual/continuous increments; tags/indexes/metadata/checksums; restart/resume/dedup; conflict authority; deletion dry runs/tombstones; reviewed non-secret configuration templates; lag/progress/failure reporting.

Exit: two real instances across disk and S3 pass interrupted seed, incremental changes, corruption rejection, retries, deletion protection for destination-only content, source outage, and destination-specific configuration preservation. Replicas remain read-only by default.

Dependencies: M02–M03 and stabilized format records. Representative tests do not replace replication compatibility coverage for every claimed format.

### M08 — Adoption and operational lifecycle

Outcome: users can deploy, migrate, operate, recover, and upgrade installations.

Scope: container/Compose and Helm; TLS/reverse proxy trust; import/export inventories and dry runs; selected repository-manager migration mappings; prewarm from lockfiles/package lists/images; storage migration; retention/eviction/GC; metadata repair/integrity checks; backup/restore; schema upgrades and rollback limitations; diagnostics; tracing; capacity planning and quotas.

Exit: documented fresh install, representative import, backup/restore, disk↔S3 migration, repair, and upgrade exercises pass with retained evidence. Images run non-root and expose only required services. Operators can detect and recover from full disks, DB failures, slow stores, and upstream outages.

Dependencies: M01–M03; final coverage requires M05 and M07. Required source migration products and versions need an explicit acceptance matrix.

### M09 — Phase 1 release qualification

Outcome: broad availability supported by reproducible evidence.

Scope: all 10 spec acceptance criteria; complete format matrix; identity/provider matrix; backend compatibility; two-site replication; threat model/security verification; performance/resource limits; API compatibility; user documentation; usability/accessibility; upgrade/recovery rehearsal and release support policy.

Exit: all release blockers closed; no unsupported claims; numeric SLOs achieved on documented hardware/workloads; release checklist records client and server versions, test results, known limitations, artifact provenance, and outstanding non-blocking issues.

Dependencies: M01–M08. Licensing/distribution remains an explicit unresolved commercial/legal choice; do not silently pick one to publish artifacts.

### M10 — Federation discovery (Phase 2, not a Phase 1 dependency)

Outcome: separately approved design and backlog for federation.

Scope: shared identity/policy, discovery, cross-site search, placement/routing, coordinated replication, and conflict semantics. Define requirements and design only after independently operable instances are proven.

Exit: a new approved scope, threat model, consistency model, migration strategy, and acceptance criteria. No Phase 1 task depends on federation services.

## Architecture scope (resolved in architecture-baseline.md)

- Artifact domain: separate feeds, sources, namespaces, components/versions, assets, immutable blobs, tags, format metadata, and provenance. Specify IDs, uniqueness, ownership, and lifecycle invariants.
- PostgreSQL: transactional boundaries, schema migration discipline, indices, job leasing, audit/event outbox, replication checkpoints, and retention. Document expected query patterns and size limits before optimization.
- Blob abstraction: context cancellation, bounded buffers, integrity verification, finalize/abort semantics, resumable transfers, and explicit backend capabilities.
- Publication: authorize and select a unique local destination, validate upload, durably store bytes, commit metadata plus audit/event records, then expose the package. Orphans are collectible; partial packages are never valid.
- Resolution: validated acyclic configuration, deterministic source precedence, separate not-found/error policies, format-defined metadata composition, cache provenance, and explain output.
- API: versioned management contract; cursor pagination and bounded filters; stable errors; conditional updates; idempotency scope/TTL/conflict behavior; generated clients and schema conformance.
- Authorization: independent read/publish/delete/configure/replicate/admin permissions; namespace/feed content selectors; explicit anonymous read; source administration; consistent machine and human identity treatment.
- Jobs/events: durable retries, cancellation, progress, scheduling, idempotency, bounded concurrency, and transactional event delivery. No requirement for an external broker until justified.
- Extension contract: format-owned routes and parsing; shared core for storage/auth/audit; explicit capability negotiation; built-in modules selected in A01.
- Security: trust boundaries for upstream URLs, redirects, credentials, signed metadata, archives, secret encryption, package clients, and replication peers. Include SSRF and decompression/resource exhaustion tests.

## Backlog shape and issue quality

GitHub milestones group release outcomes. An epic issue groups a domain; user-story issues express testable user outcomes; independently assignable implementation tasks become linked child issues. Small verification steps can remain checkboxes within a task. Use native sub-issues/dependencies where available and explicit links as the portable fallback. Do not create empty placeholder issues for the sake of counts.

Each story body must contain:

1. Stable planning ID and source spec sections.
2. “As a [persona], I want [capability], so that [outcome].”
3. Scope and explicit exclusions, with experimental/unsupported status where relevant.
4. Concrete acceptance scenarios including denied access, malformed input, cancellation, concurrency, and restart where applicable.
5. Dependencies and blocked-by relationships.
6. Links to actionable tasks and related format/architecture records.
7. Required test evidence, docs, observability, API/UI/MCP work, and migration implications.

Each task must describe a bounded deliverable, its parent story, inputs/prerequisites, acceptance checks, and completion evidence. Avoid task boundaries such as “implement all storage” or “support npm” with no workflow decomposition.

Backlog labels: `type:epic`, `type:story`, `type:task`, `type:decision`, `type:conformance`; `phase:0`, `phase:1`, `phase:2`; `status:planning`, `status:blocked`, `status:ready`; domain labels for core, storage, formats, identity, API, UI, MCP, cache, replication, operations, adoption, and quality. Milestones carry release order; priorities carry business urgency. Do not assign people or dates without agreement.

## Definition of ready

A task is ready when its parent outcome is accepted, dependencies have passed their gates, open decisions that affect implementation are resolved, acceptance scenarios are executable, test dependencies/fixtures exist or are explicitly part of the task, and it has no unacknowledged scope assumptions. Global planning readiness is additionally required before any first task starts.

## Definition of done

- Behavior satisfies the story's positive and negative acceptance criteria.
- Relevant unit, real PostgreSQL integration, backend contract, protocol-client, and end-to-end tests pass; concurrency/large-object tests are included where they test actual risks.
- API schema, capability ledger, operator/client documentation, and UI/MCP surfaces reflect the implemented behavior.
- Authorization and audit are enforced; no credential leakage; operational metrics and actionable failures exist.
- Migrations, interruption/restart behavior, cleanup, and compatibility implications are reviewed.
- Evidence links record tested versions and backend/client combinations. Code merged is not by itself evidence of format conformance.

## Release evidence matrix

For each format, select representative and boundary clients with pinned test versions; document supported version ranges separately. Cover publish/consume, update/delete, source selection, cache freshness, upstream failure, authentication, checksums/signatures, metadata composition, range/resume where meaningful, and replication. Unsupported/inapplicable cells require a reason.

Cross-cutting suites include:

- Storage: identical digest, lifecycle, cancellation, multipart, corruption, and GC-reference scenarios for disk and primary MinIO, with the same reusable suite for additional S3 providers.
- Concurrency: cold fan-out, simultaneous immutable publishes, refresh races, deletion versus active reads, job leases, and interrupted replication.
- Identity: Zitadel plus another OIDC provider; agreed SAML/LDAP profiles; scoped tokens, revoked/expired credentials, group mapping, anonymous denial, and emergency recovery.
- Interfaces: each administrative capability through API, then UI and MCP parity; OpenAPI validation and generated-client compatibility.
- Reliability: DB unavailable, full disk, slow/unavailable object store, upstream outage, restart mid-upload, restart mid-job, and restore on a clean installation.
- Performance: warm/cold pulls, large blobs/models/layers, metadata-heavy clients, high fan-out, bounded-memory transfers, and accurate cache savings.

## Spec traceability

| Specification | Planned coverage |
|---|---|
| §1–4 vision, goals, boundaries, personas | M00 scope and all story personas; Phase 2 separation |
| §5 ecosystem breadth and adapter contract | M00 capability ledger, M04–M05, M09 conformance |

| §6.5 build acceleration | M03 caching/prewarm/metrics/quotas, M08 runner/adoption guidance |
| §6.6 storage | M01 PostgreSQL, M02 disk/S3, M08 migration/repair |
| §6.7 replication | M07, M09 two-instance evidence |
| §6.8 federation | M10 only |

| §6.10 governance | M01 authorization/audit, M06 integrations/events, M08 retention/export |

| §6.12 UI | M06 and incremental domain screens |
| §6.13 operations | M01 diagnostics, M08 deployments/lifecycle, M09 rehearsals |
| §7 architecture | M00 decisions, M01–M03 contracts, M07 replication |
| §8 performance/reliability | M03 baseline, M09 numeric release gates |
| §9 import/export/adoption | M08 |
| §10 delivery phases | M00 = Phase 0; M01–M09 = Phase 1; M10 = Phase 2 |
| §11 acceptance 1–2 | M04–M05 format workflows and M09 evidence |
| §11 acceptance 3–4 | M01/M06 identity, permission, and audit parity |
| §11 acceptance 5–6 | M07 replication and M02 backend contracts |
| §11 acceptance 7–9 | M08 adoption/recovery, M03/M09 performance |
| §11 acceptance 10 | M00 ledger and M09 evidence gate |
| §12 open decisions/risks | Decision register below and capability records |

## Confirmed decision log

- D001: PostgreSQL only for all installations. Owner response, 2026-10-18.
- D002: No license selection at present. Owner response, 2026-10-18.
- D003: Complete planning and GitHub backlog before implementation. Owner instruction, 2026-10-18.

- D007: Primary validation is OKE plus MinIO on TrueNAS SCALE; AWS and other providers remain supported targets. Reuse compatibility tests without creating test environments for every provider. Owner clarification, 2026-10-18.

## Delivery and support evidence

OCI/Docker → Go → Helm → Cargo → Raw, then remaining formats. OCI artifacts retain a separate conformance record after Raw. All 26 remain Phase 1 release requirements.

T1 records protocol decisions, selected clients, source/composition behavior, non-goals and positive/negative cases. T2–T4 deliver protocol implementation, cache/lifecycle integration and real-client evidence. Closing T1 does not imply support. A supported workflow must have passing retained results and exact artifact versions.

Run shared backend tests against disk and primary MinIO. AWS and other S3 providers remain compatibility targets using the same suite; do not create environments for every vendor or a full client×backend×provider matrix.


# Shared format contract rules

Status: Engineering contracts selected for implementation on 2026-10-18. No adapter is implemented or certified by this planning work. These rules plus each Fxx record replace open-ended workflow candidates; implementation tasks supply evidence before any support claim.

## Source, routing and publication contract

All 26 formats have local delivery, remote pull-through and replica delivery in scope. Local publication is either a native ecosystem publish operation or the explicit admin-ingestion workflow in its record; unsupported native commands are not advertised. An ingestion request creates a staged publish session through the management API, uploads declared assets, validates their closure, then commits metadata/indexes atomically. Requests are authenticated/scoped and idempotent. The React console and MCP use these same operations.

Writes resolve to one local source before data acceptance and never implicitly forward upstream. Immutable versions default to conflict on different bytes. Deletion/overwrite/retention is policy-controlled and produces audit/outbox events. Local signing keys are separate from upstream trust keys. No generic union of signed repository metadata is permitted.

`package-owner`, `path-owner`, `object-owner` and `snapshot-owner` select an ownership unit. Explicit namespace bindings outrank source order; a selected owner stays fixed across metadata and byte retrieval. Fallback may choose an owner on initial not-found, never silently replace a missing version from another owner. Snapshot sources are coherent generations. More permissive composition must be added as an explicit adapter capability with conformance evidence.

## Cache and authentication contract

Default metadata TTL is 5 minutes, negative-cache TTL 30 seconds; digest-addressed immutable blobs live until retention. An adapter tightens freshness for mutable indexes. Cache keys include source/normalized identity/representation/generation plus authorization domain where needed. Unauthorized results are not global misses. Stale-if-error/offline is opt-in, respects signature validity and is visible through explain/metrics. Coalesced streaming, cancellation and range support use the shared core where protocol semantics allow.

TLS is required for deployed clients. Native registry token/API-key/basic schemes map to shared scoped identities; browser sessions never replace package-client authentication. Anonymous read is opt-in. Signing, integrity, client auth and uploader provenance are separate controls. Archive metadata parsing must be bounded and must not execute uploaded code or follow unsafe paths.

## Lifecycle and replication contract

Each adapter maps component identity/version, asset roles/digests, tags, raw metadata, search fields and retained references into the shared domain. Search is scoped and paginated. A full feed seed includes cached artifacts, indexes, tags and metadata unless an explicit selective policy excludes them. Preflight reports unresolved external references; it cannot claim a complete offline replica until required dependency/source archives are materialized. Replicas preserve exact immutable byte identities and authoritative ownership. Tombstones never remove destination-only assets.

Each adapter implements metadata-aware cleanup and health checks plus publish/resolve/cache/validation metrics. Read explain and publish routing diagnostics must be available in API, UI and MCP. Distinct forms of deletion (unlist/yank/tag removal/blob dereference) remain format-specific.

## Conformance evidence required during implementation

1. Execute the pinned baseline clients and positive/negative cases in the individual record; store exact binary/image digests in the harness lockfile at fixture installation. A reference version is a test target, not evidence already obtained.
2. Exercise local publish/ingest then consume, same-endpoint native read/write where defined, remote cold/warm/cache freshness, source ownership, token denial, signature/hash failures, malformed archives, cancellation/restart and concurrent immutable conflicts.
3. Run shared backend scenarios first on disk and the owner's MinIO. Use the same suite for AWS/other compatible endpoints only when needed; do not construct a provider fleet or a full client×backend×provider Cartesian matrix.
4. Verify seed plus incremental metadata/tag/index changes, restart and source outage; every record requires offline closure or an explicit visibly incomplete result.
5. Retain versioned fixtures/results/limitations and document exact client setup. Platform-specific clients use macOS/Windows runners only for their format cases. No support claim before evidence.

Protocol-specific requirements derive from linked official references. Scope, ownership policy and excluded non-goals are Kuvryn Ant engineering choices. Exclusions cannot remove an explicit spec requirement; all 26 ecosystems remain Phase 1 release blockers.
